title: Nvidia CEO Pours $75M Into San Francisco Art Campus
description:
News
                Vanderbilt University's building on the ruins of the California College of the Arts will bear the billionai
body:
News
                Vanderbilt University's building on the ruins of the California College of the Arts will bear the billionaire's name   
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang on January 5, 2026 (photo Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
    
        
            Vanderbilt University's new San Francisco arts and design campus will bear the name of Nvidia co-founder Jensen (Jen-Hsun) Huang after the billionaire committed millions to the institution. The university announced this week that the AI chipmaker and his wife, Lori Huang, gifted $75 million to establish the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design.The controversial campus will replace the nearly 120-year-old California College of the Arts (CCA), San Francisco's last remaining private art school. The beloved nonprofit institution, which grants bachelor's and master's degrees across artistic disciplines, was purchased by Vanderbilt amid financial struggles caused by a decline in enrollment and a growing budget deficit.The Huangs donated a $22.5 million matching gift to CCA in February 2025 to help stabilize the institution's shaky finances. However, not even a full year later, CCA announced that it would cease operating after the 2026–2027 academic year, and that the Potrero Hill campus would be subsumed by Vanderbilt. Not everyone in the local art community is happy with Huang's donation. "These billionaires would much rather play God and remake our art schools in their own image than support a 120-year-old legacy fine art school," Lindsey White, a San Francisco-based artist, educator, and CCA alum, told Hyperallergic."In both CCA and SFAI cases, billionaires with zero experience in the arts have taken over major real estate, leaving local artists, educators, and workers in a dystopian nightmare," White continued. "Sadly, it seems our local government didn't see the value in saving the last fine art school in Northern California either."California Governor Gavin Newsom had worked to secure a $20 million public grant in 2025 to keep the private institution afloat despite significant opposition from state lawmakers. At the time, the governor argued that though it was atypical for the government to fund a private college, the state should fund CCA to safeguard its cultural sector amid Trump's attacks on the arts. He later expressed shock at the school's closure, but critics said he should've seen it coming. Huang co-founded Nvidia, a manufacturer of graphics processing units (GPUs) now widely used to power artificial intelligence programs, in a Denny's restaurant booth in 1993. In May, the chipmaker reached a valuation of $5.5 trillion, the highest in the history of publicly traded companies. According to the university's announcement, the Huangs donated the large sum out of their belief that "creative practice [is] one of innovation’s most essential engines."“Technology expands what we can build," Jensen Huang said in the press release issued earlier this week. "Art and design determine why we build it. Together they shape civilization."In an op-ed about the closure of CCA in the San Francisco Chronicle earlier this year, local gallerist Griff Williams warned that "corporate interests seem to eclipse all else in San Francisco.""Mayor Lurie, the closure of the California College of the Arts is a tragedy for the city, not a 'win,'" he wrote. "It’s another blow to the legacy of the heroes who made San Francisco unique: Joan Brown, David Ireland, Bruce Conner, Hung Liu, Hank Willis Thomas, Dewey Crumpler, Robert Arneson, Manuel Neri, Harrell Fletcher, Jim Goldberg, Viola Frey, Ted Purves, Dodie Bellamy and Susan O’Malley, to name a few."

title: Joyce Kozloff Reveals Herself as  Guerrilla Girls Founding Member
description:
News
                After decades of anonymity, the feminist artist and activist disclosed in an interview that she is the woman beh
body:
News
                After decades of anonymity, the feminist artist and activist disclosed in an interview that she is the woman behind the mask of “Liubov Popova.” 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Joyce Kozloff attends the opening reception for Local Editions: Prints by New York Artists (2018) at the Metropolitan Museum of Art (photo Taylor Hill via Getty Images)Artist and activist Joyce Kozloff has taken off the mask after 41 years, disclosing in a new interview with Art Journal Open that she was among the founding members of the Guerrilla Girls. She also revealed that “Liubov Popova” was her assigned pseudonym within the collective, whose members took the names of late women artists to maintain their own anonymity. In 2016, she published a (sneaky) biographical essay in Hyperallergic that both examined and lauded the Russian artist's creative evolution and career milestones throughout her unfortunately short life. “Remaining anonymous was an important Guerrilla Girls decision,” Kozloff explained to curators Maura Reilly and Helena Reckitt during her tell-all in the American magazine's Feminist Interview Project. “People thought this was to avoid art world reprisals. For me, that was never the reason. I argued for anonymity because I didn’t want attention to be on us as individuals, I wanted it to remain on the issues.”The artist said that she and two others were among the seven inaugural Guerrilla Girls who had lived through the women's movement in the 1970s, and that the younger women in the collective proclaimed that people had become disinterested with feminism, outlining a need for updated language and visuals. Having moved to Los Angeles when her husband Max began teaching at the California Institute of the Arts, Kozloff joined a feminist “consciousness raising” group that quickly radicalized her in 1971. This experience gave way to her role in co-organizing the Los Angeles Council of Women Artists (LACWA) that protested the paucity of female representation at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.Kozloff's role in the feminist art movement expanded upon her return to New York in the early '70s — she was among the inaugural members of the Heresies Collective, and her art practice and shift to public art bolstered the emerging Pattern and Decoration movement.LACWA's data-driven protest model laid the basic framework for the Guerrilla Girls, which got its name after a new member misunderstood the title and brought a (now signature) gorilla mask to a meeting. Among the group's debut interventions was an ad campaign calling out the disparity between the number of women artists shown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art versus the number of displayed artworks depicting nude women.The group's confrontational wheat-pasted posters directly named and shamed institutions, galleries, and collectors that maintained sexist and racist hierarchies, drawing immense publicity and curiosity about the Guerrilla Girls' identities. “People were pissed and wanted to out us,” Kozloff told Reckitt and Reilly, adding that she was affiliated with the Guerrilla Girls until 1991. A printed reproduction of the Guerrilla Girls' “The Advantages of Being a Woman Artist” (1988) at the 2018 Gowanus Open Studios (photo Alissa Guzman/Hyperallergic)The artist also revealed her hand in developing one of the collective's most iconic poster campaigns — “The Advantages of Being a Woman Artist” (1988). She told Art Journal Open that the project was born from her time in a residency house she shared with married male artists who had brought their younger affair partners along as homemakers and unpaid studio assistants.“When I got back, I wrote a rough draft, 'The Disadvantages of Being a Woman Artist,'” Kozloff explained. “Until then, our posters always had verifiable statistics, so this was a stretch. But then, our clever members turned it around to 'Advantages,' and it worked!”Four decades on, Kozloff thinks that there has been enormous progress in the representation of women in the arts sphere. But, she said, “I'm very much more concerned about the current threats to women’s progress in the larger political realm,” citing the overturning of Roe v. Wade, the far-right push to keep women at home, and the beauty industry's invasive emphasis on youthful appearances.“But we can’t tell the next generation what to do, they will find their own ways,” she left off.

title: Christopher Nolan, David Hockney, Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara
description:
Weekly Newsletter
                A political prisoner is freed, a Homerist reviews Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” and do we have to pre
body:
Weekly Newsletter
                A political prisoner is freed, a Homerist reviews Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” and do we have to pretend to like David Hockney’s iPad paintings?
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            After five years in a maximum-security prison outside Havana, Cuban dissident artist Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara was released and exiled to Miami. He's a free man now, but there's not much to celebrate. The US continues to choke the island, driving its people into despair. Justice is scarce both here and there.Meanwhile, everyone's talking about Christopher Nolan's film adaptation of The Odyssey, so we got a certified Homerist to review the film for us. "As a spectacle, the movie is a fantastic success," writes Joel P. Christensen of CUNY Graduate Center. "As a reflection of us, it fails."Now to a delicate subject: the late David Hockney's iPad paintings. Yes, the tablet device allowed him to continue making art in his sunset years, but must we pretend to like the outcome even if we don't? Our London critic Olivia McEwan thinks not.Scroll down to read about the political message behind a giant wiener in Times Square, the short-spined raccoon that became the darling of misfits everywhere, and the intense backlash over a Hollywood star's pair of earrings. Thanks for reading. I think I'll go see The Odyssey this weekend.—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

	
		
			Zendaya’s Earrings Are Part of a Much Bigger Problem
		
	
	
		Zendaya faced backlash for wearing a pair of 3,000-year-old Iranian gold discs at a London photocall for Christopher Nolan’s forthcoming adaptation of The Odyssey earlier this month. The discs, mounted in 18-karat gold and diamonds, were recently made into earrings by jeweler Glenn Spiro as part of his Materials of the Old World collection, and subsequently acquired by London jewelry house Barron London, who stated that they are part of the company’s private collection and not for sale. However, they did not belong on the red carpet at all. 
      
Described as a “voracious collector,” mesmerized by special artifacts “regardless of their provenance,” Spiro said in an interview about the collection, “You can wear something around your neck that dates back thousands of years but is still contemporary and cool.” One online review of Spiro’s collection perfectly captures the performative exoticism driving this kind of repurposing: “... fragments of forgotten empires are not merely displayed but reborn.”
	
	
		Read More
	


                    
                    
                    
                        
                            Indie Film From the Global Majority: BlackStar Celebrates 15 Years of Cinema for LiberationThe world’s most significant and groundbreaking filmmakers of color will gather to showcase their work in Philadelphia August 6-9.
                        
                        
                            Learn more
                        
                    
            NewsThe Art Institute of Chicago plans to transfer its in-house custodial workforce to a private contractor in August, drawing outcry from unionized workers.Cuban dissident performance artist Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara arrived in Miami after over a week of ambiguity surrounding his whereabouts following his scheduled release from a five-year sentence for “contempt, defamation, and public disorder.”New York Chinatown residents and activists protested outside a town hall event at the Museum of Chinese in America, condemning the leadership’s acceptance of a $35 million grant from the city that they believe is tied to the construction of a borough jail.Following a legal battle between the city of Philadelphia and the Trump administration, federal officials replaced exhibits describing the history of slavery in the United States at a Pennsylvania historical park.  A newly shared letter reveals that alleged “racist” and “culturally insensitive” behaviors contributed to Yuko Kikuchi’s January resignation from her post as head of academic programs at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.Tate names Jessica Morgan, who led the Dia Art Foundation in New York for over a decade, as its next director.Two painters are suing The Hole Gallery, alleging that it owes them a combined sum of about $50,000 in outstanding sales proceeds.Collectors Anne and Arthur Goldstein gift over 70 works of modern and contemporary art to the Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers University.Dmitriy Popov was handed a 20-year sentence over the fatal stabbing of Black gay professional dancer O’Shae Sibley. The sentencing comes after Popov was convicted of manslaughter as a hate crime in June.Just weeks before a historic collection of 20th-century Mexican art is slated to leave the country for an exhibition in Europe, a group of advocates is suing Mexico’s principal cultural entity over allegations regarding the legal basis for exporting the nation’s artistic heritage.Just a few months after the reopening of the New Museum’s expanded building, a water leak shut down the Manhattan institution for a full weekend.The New York Foundation for the Arts awards $903,000 to 132 artists across New York State in its joint fellowship program with the New York State Council on the Arts.Art Movements: Michael Wellen and José Luis Blondet are the curators of the next Made in L.A., Tate names a new director, and the Immigrant Artist Biennial is back for another edition.
From Our Critics

	
		
			The Sunflower Effect of Kyung-Me
		
	
	
		The artist’s current series marks a shift in her practice, evoking the life span of a sunflower — from blooming to dying, from sharply defined forms to rivulets of dissolution. | John Yau
	
	
		Read More
	

Features
Required Reading: The Louvre reopens the room where it happens, a Texas artist’s outdoor collection, Nancy Drew in the public domain, Rachel Cusk and Natalie Portman have beef, and more.In Memoriam: we honor Christine Borland, an artist who explored human fragility through science; Astrid Furnival, a pioneering British textile artist; Vicente Matallana, a champion of digital art, and more.A View From the Easel: Patrick Guetta repurposes brand imagery to spread environmentalist messages and approaches the streets of Los Angeles as mini museums in themselves.

title: President Trump Orders Signs Installed Outside Smithsonian Warning Public of ‘Inaccurate Information’
description: President Donald Trump escalated his battle with the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History Friday, ordering signage outside the institut
body:
President Donald Trump escalated his battle with the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History Friday, ordering signage outside the institution to flag what an executive order calls “inaccurate information” presented in its exhibits.

	The extraordinary directive comes amid intensifying Republican scrutiny of the Smithsonian branch, which was the subject of a recent 162-page report accusing its director, Anthea M. Hartig, of replacing “historical education” with “extreme political activism.” According to the order, the signage will tell visitors that the museum’s exhibits “should be renovated” to align with the report and direct them to locations where, in the administration’s view, American history is more accurately reflected. The administration did not specify which locations the signage would direct visitors to.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Trump’s order comes only days after Hartig faced two congressional hearings over alleged political bias in her museum’s curation and questions about her loyalty to the United States. Hartig, an explicit target of the White House report, rejected its central claims, defending the museum’s scholarship as “rigorous” and “fact-based” and saying it aims to tell a fuller story of America through “historical evidence, competing perspectives” and “enduring debates.”

	The directive also ordered several high-ranking government officials, including the Secretary of the Interior and the director of the Office of Management and Budget, to “restore trust in the Smithsonian Institution” and ensure its compliance with the White House’s findings. As first noted by the New York Times, the inclusion of the budget office appears to reference the Smithsonian’s reliance on federal funding. The directive also named the assistant to the president for domestic policy, whose Domestic Policy Council published the White House’s report on the Smithsonian.

	Friday’s directive cited President Trump’s March 2025 executive order, “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History,” which accused the Smithsonian of failing to properly celebrate “the remarkable achievements of the United States” by casting “its founding principles and historical milestones in a negative light,” particularly ahead of the country’s 250th anniversary earlier this month.
	

	Citing the museum’s failure to “appropriately honor” the “signers of the Declaration of Independence,” Trump has now directed government agencies to “install temporary exhibits or signage on N.P.S.-maintained sidewalks, walkways, and land used by the public” to correct what it calls “inaccurate information presented in the museum.”

	Representative Melanie Stansbury (Democrat of New Mexico) objected to the order in a statement published by the Times, saying, “Once again, the Trump administration is attempting to use executive authority to exercise its political will over our nation’s independent cultural institutions.”

	Stansbury also objected to the congressional proceedings this week, calling the Republican-led campaign against the Smithsonian a “political witch hunt” while announcing new legislation aimed at asserting congressional authority over the institution and similar independent agencies. She described Friday’s executive order as “a clear political overreach, driven by an ideological agenda to rewrite American history. Our Smithsonian institutions do not belong to the president, but to the American people, and neither does our national story.”

schema.headline: President Trump Orders Signs Installed Outside Smithsonian Warning Public of ‘Inaccurate Information’

title: Thieves Snatch 2,500-Year-Old Celtic Gold Torque from French Museum in Broad Daylight
description: A 2,500-year-old gold collar belonging to the Vix Treasure archaeological find was stolen Friday in broad daylight from a French museum, according t
body:
A 2,500-year-old gold collar belonging to the Vix Treasure archaeological find was stolen Friday in broad daylight from a French museum, according to reports in Le Parisien and France 3.

	The thieves allegedly entered the Musée du Pays Châtillonnais – Trésor de Vix in Châtillon-sur-Seine, Burgundy, around 10:30 a.m. on July 24 by paying the admission fee, acting as regular visitors to the museum. Dijon prosecutor Olivier Caracotch said in a statement to Le Parisien that the thieves smashed the display case holding the gold collar, called a torque, before fleeing the museum through the main entrance.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Caracotch added that his office has opened an investigation for organized crime and that the Juridiction interrégionale spécialisée (JIRS) in Nancy will assist “given this classification, the nature of the facts, and the great complexity of the procedure.”  

	Jérémie Brigand, the mayor of Châtillon-sur-Seine and president of Communauté de Communes du Pays Châtillonnais, said in a statement, according to Le Parisien, that the museum had faced “two previous failed nighttime burglary attempts” in the past eight months. The museum said that it had upped its security as a result, spending some €150,000 ($171,000) on new security cameras, motion detectors, and door detectors, per the France 3 report.

	 “Despite these measures, the perpetrators demonstrated an organization, a speed of execution and a determination that allowed them to carry out their action,” he said in his Le Parisien statement, characterizing the theft as an “attack on cultural heritage and the public interest.”

	He told France 3 that the stolen torque is “priceless, it’s a unique piece in the world. And beyond the value of the gold, it’s a historical piece of Châtillonnais heritage. And it’s really damaging and regrettable that criminals are attacking the history of the Châtillonnais and our country.”

	The torque theft recalls the brazen theft at the Louvre in Paris, in which thieves made off with $102 million worth of jewels in less than eight minutes, also in broad daylight. That high-profile theft ultimately caused the museum’s president to resign and expedited the Louvre’s plans to address its dated security systems, which the museum is expected to begin in January 2027. The Louvre’s Apollo Gallery, where the stolen crown jewels had been on display, reopened this week without the jewels, which are still missing.
	

	The Louvre heist led to several other museums across France facing similar thefts. Earlier this month, thieves targeted another French museum, stealing some $4.57 million worth of jewels from the Lalique Museum in Wingen-sur-Moder, Alsace.

	The Vix Treasure was discovered in 1953 at the foot of Mont Lassois, near the village of Vix, or about 4 miles north of Châtillon-sur-Seine, where the museum is located, according to its website. The heart of the findings was the tomb of a woman, called the “Dame of Vix” (Princess of Vix), who is believed to have been buried between 470 and 460 BCE.

	The tomb was filled with precious objects, including the golden torque, which is made of 24-karat gold, weighs just over a pound, and dates to the 6th century BCE; the Vix Krater, which includes a depiction of Medusa and was produced around 530 BCE in the Greek colony of Sybaris in southern Italy and it is unknown how it came to Vix; and the Silver Phiale, likely a ceremonial item that is the “oldest silver vase discovered north of the Alps.”  

	The golden torque is of a Celtic design in the shape of an arc “with its two ends resting on a lion paw that is positioned on hollow spheres,” per the museum, which notes that it was a symbol of power. Atop each lion paw is a depiction of the winged horse Pegasus, representing the Greek influence on the region during the era. That influence is juxtaposed with Celtic imagery of “two pear-shaped balls [that] symbolize the sun.”  
	

	Initially, the torque was discovered on the princess’s skull and believed to be a diadem, but further research confirmed that it was “worn around the neck, like a necklace, by a member of the aristocracy. Its placement in the tomb likely resulted from the tomb’s collapse shortly after the burial,” per the museum.  

	The museum adds, “Through its iconographic elements and method of manufacture, the torque reflects a blend of cultures and a transfer of technology, illustrating the vibrant trade in Europe at the end of the First Iron Age.”

schema.headline: Thieves Snatch 2,500-Year-Old Celtic Gold Torque from French Museum in Broad Daylight

title: Forgotten in French Customs for Decades, a Chagall Finds New Home in Museum Near Swiss Border
description: Earlier this week, French customs near the Swiss border gifted an artwork by Marc Chagall to a nearby museum in France, after it had been languishin
body:
Earlier this week, French customs near the Swiss border gifted an artwork by Marc Chagall to a nearby museum in France, after it had been languishing in bureaucratic purgatory, forgotten on a warehouse shelf for over 20 years, reported ICI Besançon.

	In 2006, French authorities stopped a truck carrying artworks from France into Switzerland, and seized an etching by Chagall, along with a 1959 drawing by modern sculptor and painter Ossip Zadkine, because they lacked required certificates for removing them from the country. The two people transporting the works were arrested and fined for hiding the artworks, according to the Times of London. Afterwards, both artworks were effectively forgotten for nearly 20 years due to the “weight of bureaucracy,” per one source speaking to the Times.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	That oversight has now been rectified. On Monday, the eastern Franche-Comté region’s customs office donated the 1924 Chagall etching, titled “L’Acrobate au violon” [Acrobat with Violin], to the Musée des Beaux-Arts et d’Archéologie de Besançon.

Besançon Museum of Fine Arts Showcasing its 1st work by Marc Chagall“The Acrobat with the Violin” (1924), seized in 2006 following an attempt to illegally export it to Switzerland, was donated to the museum by the Franche-Comté Regional Customs Office. pic.twitter.com/RcWgGZTfcm— La Gazette Drouot – International (@Gazette_Inter) July 21, 2026


	The Chagall depicts the Russian-French artist’s characteristic, often surreal motifs. At its center is a man lithely balancing atop a violin, beside a floating, upside-down chicken. A goat-like animal stands on its front legs in the foreground, as its body bends back into the air, and it appears to be playing the violin. A small Jewish Star of David can be seen on the man’s right pant leg.

	“You can clearly recognize Chagall in this somewhat dreamlike style, this dream world that is very detached from reality,” said Maël Vandewalle, curator at the Besançon museum, who also helped authenticate the artwork. Issued as an edition of 150, the Chagall etching is estimated to be worth only a few thousand euros, but it is the first and only piece by Chagall to enter the Besançon museum collection, where it will go on view in September. “The customs service has really honored us,” said Ludovic Fagaut, the town mayor. 

	Chagall’s highest auction record is for a 1928 painting, Les Amoureux [The Lovers], that sold at Sotheby’s in New York for $28.45 million in 2017. As for the Zadkine drawing, which also touches on a musical theme, with a depiction of a man playing a guitar, it was given to the Musée Zadkine in Paris.

schema.headline: Forgotten in French Customs for Decades, a Chagall Finds New Home in Museum Near Swiss Border

title: Archie Rand’s Landmark Letter Paintings Acquired by Italy’s Modena FC Collection
description: For decades, Archie Rand‘s “Letter Paintings” series has been something of a cult favorite among painters and critics. Now, 44 of them are heading t
body:
For decades, Archie Rand‘s “Letter Paintings” series has been something of a cult favorite among painters and critics. Now, 44 of them are heading to an unlikely home: the corporate collection of Italy’s Modena FC.

	New York–based gallery Jarvis Art announced this week that the Italian football club has acquired the group of paintings, which Rand made between 1968 and 1971 while still a teenager. The series was shown in 1983 at the Museum of the Carnegie Institute and reunited in a 1991 exhibition at Exit Art in New York, where it earned a jazzy review from New York Times critic Roberta Smith. The works have rarely been seen together since.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	The paintings marked an early turning point for Rand. As a teenager, he apprenticed under painter Larry Poons and became an acolyte of the influential critic Clement Greenberg, who saw the young artist as part of the next generation of abstract painters. But instead of following that path to its logical conclusion, Rand veered off script. He began writing the names of the musicians, poets, artists, and public figures he loved across luminous abstract canvases, turning Color Field painting into something deeply personal.


			
			
			
	
			
					Archie Rand, LaVern Baker, 1969.
	



	Looking back years later, Rand described the works as “tombstones for the unheralded.” They were, he said, an attempt to paint something modern art had largely forgotten: love.

	In her review, Smith argued the paintings deserved far more attention than they had received. She praised the way they fused the lush surfaces of Color Field painting with the language and references of Conceptual art, calling them works that balanced “reverence and irreverence.” She went on to suggest they anticipated later developments ranging from New Image Painting to Jean-Michel Basquiat’s use of musicians’ names.

	“This acquisition of one of Archie’s most prominent historical series, along with the great success of his recent show at the gallery, Heads, is a testament to the longevity of his work, not just today but throughout his career,” said Lindsay Jarvis, founder of Jarvis Art.

schema.headline: Archie Rand’s Landmark Letter Paintings Acquired by Italy’s Modena FC Collection
